items.title: Repo skeleton: pyproject, src layout, ruff, pytest
items.description: Python 3.12+ project with src/wonderland layout. uv for envs. ruff for lint/format. pytest. Pre-commit optional for now.

items.title: Utterance schema
items.description: Pydantic model for Utterance per WONDERLAND_SPEC §4: id (ULID), thread_id, parent_id, speaker, addressed_to, speech_act, content (body+artifacts), references, timestamp, confidence, stance, affect. SpeechAct enum. AgentIdentity, Stance, AffectVector subtypes.

items.title: Identity schema and constitution loader
items.description: Identity dataclass: name, version, constitution (from constitutions/<name>.md), interests (speech_act subscription set), engagement_policy hook. Loader parses YAML/markdown frontmatter from constitutions/.

items.title: Caucus event bus over Redis Streams
items.description: Caucus class wrapping Redis Streams. publish(utterance), subscribe(interests) -> async iterator. Per-thread consumer groups. Replay support for debugging. Local in-memory fake for tests.

items.title: Episodic memory store (SQLite)
items.description: Per-agent SQLite at <project_root>/.wonderland/memory/<agent>/episodic.sqlite. Schema: utterances observed/produced, indexed by thread_id and timestamp. Query by thread/topic/other-agent.

items.title: Anthropic client wrapper with prompt caching
items.description: Thin wrapper around anthropic SDK. Default model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001. Cache_control on the constitution + relational memory layers of composed context. Token accounting hook for budget telemetry.

items.title: WonderlandAgent base class
items.description: Per WONDERLAND_SPEC §5: identity, memory, bus, listen()/speak() loop. should_engage hook delegating to identity.engagement_policy. compose_context(triggers) producing layered prompt. deliberate(context) calling LLM. Sometimes returns None (silence is valid).

items.title: Layered context composer
items.description: compose_context assembles: [CONSTITUTION]+[RELATIONSHIPS]+[CURRENT THREAD]+[TRIGGER]+[YOUR MOVE]. Constitution and relationships are the cache prefix. Returns Anthropic messages format with cache_control breakpoints.

items.title: Engagement policy: heuristic-then-LLM
items.description: engagement_policy(utterance, memory) -> bool. Heuristic pass first (cheap; speech_act in interests, addressed_to match, thread_state). Optional LLM tiebreak only when heuristic is uncertain. Per-agent overrides in constitution metadata.

items.title: Cheshire Cat agent — first end-to-end
items.description: Concrete WonderlandAgent for the Cat. Loads constitutions/cheshire_cat.md. ADR writer artifact handler (writes to .wonderland/architecture/adr-NNN.md). End-to-end test: directive -> Cat produces proposal -> ADR file appears.

items.title: ADR writer and registry
items.description: Service that takes an ADR artifact from a Cat proposal and writes it to .wonderland/architecture/adr-NNN-<slug>.md with auto-incrementing N. Validates Tradeoffs section is present (the grin is non-optional).

items.title: Semantic memory layer
items.description: Per-agent semantic store: distilled beliefs about codebase, domain, other agents. Compaction job runs between threads. Markdown-backed for legibility, SQLite index for queries.

items.title: Relational memory layer
items.description: Per-agent relational notes keyed by other-agent name. The Caterpillar's notes on Tweedledee differ from his notes on Tweedledum. Used as part of cache prefix in compose_context.

items.title: White Rabbit agent
items.description: Concrete WonderlandAgent for the Rabbit. Loads constitutions/white_rabbit.md. Ticket artifact handler (writes tickets — format TBD by his constitution). Engagement: directive, story, proposal touching scope, concern about timeline.

items.title: Two-agent integration test (Cat + Rabbit)
items.description: Test scenario: Dodo issues directive -> Rabbit decomposes into tickets -> Cat issues reframe on architecturally-implicating ticket -> Rabbit revises. Verify role boundaries hold (no Cat-tickets, no Rabbit-ADRs).

items.title: Compaction-as-agent-behavior mechanism
items.description: Per WONDERLAND_SPEC §8: 'compaction is itself an agent behavior.' Hook that asks each agent to reflect-and-distill between threads, in-character. Hatter's reflections are nonlinear, Caterpillar's are slow/categorical.

items.title: Dodo orchestrator
items.description: Per WONDERLAND_SPEC §6. publish(directive), observe(thread_id) yielding thread state. Loads constitutions/dodo.md. Doesn't direct — watches.

items.title: Quiescence detection
items.description: Detect 'phase done' as relevant agents stopping publishing on a thread. Heuristic: no new utterances for N seconds AND all engaged agents have issued at least one terminal speech_act (deference, observation closing concern, etc.). Tunable per-thread.

items.title: Stuck and deadlock detection
items.description: Stuck: a thread has open questions/concerns with no answer for too long. Deadlock: two or more agents disagreeing in a tight loop, no path to resolution. Triggers Dodo intervention or human escalation per spec §7.

items.title: Conflict resolution: domain primacy + dissent record
items.description: Per WONDERLAND_SPEC §7. Each speech_act has an owning domain. Dodo (or composer) resolves cross-agent conflict by domain owner; dissent is recorded as a structured artifact attached to the resolution. Multi-domain composition path for genuine spans.

items.title: Human-in-the-loop escalation
items.description: When Dodo declares deadlock: emit structured escalation with directive, conflicting proposals, suggested resolution, explicit decision-question. Human reply is recorded as a directive-with-reasoning that future threads inherit as precedent.

items.title: Showcase 1: /health endpoint directive
items.description: End-to-end small directive per WONDERLAND_SPEC §10. Add a /health endpoint to a Phoenix app. Full loop: Dodo directive -> Alice/Rabbit/Cat/Tweedles/Hatter all visible. Recorded transcript. ~2 min runtime target.

items.title: Project init CLI: wonderland init
items.description: Bootstrap .wonderland/ in a target project: create directory layout, copy stub configs, register Redis stream prefixes for the project. Mirrors 'daedalus init' pattern.

items.title: Alice agent
items.description: Concrete WonderlandAgent for Alice. User-story generation from inhabited personas. Engagement: directive, ticket if user-impact unclear, proposal if user-need at stake.

items.title: Mad Hatter agent
items.description: Concrete WonderlandAgent for the Hatter. Test-scenario generation. Sideways thinking. Engagement: nearly everything (per his constitution); selectively interjects.

items.title: Caterpillar agent
items.description: Concrete WonderlandAgent for the Caterpillar. Code review on every implementation. Differentiated relational notes per Tweedle. Speech act: review.

items.title: Queen of Hearts agent
items.description: Concrete WonderlandAgent for the Queen. Security and compliance ruling. Engagement triggered when she 'smells blood' — credentials, auth, data residency, injection vectors.

items.title: Dormouse agent
items.description: Concrete WonderlandAgent for the Dormouse. SRE/observability. Mostly silent; wakes on production-implicating events. Owns dashboard/alert/runbook artifacts.

items.title: Tweedledee agent (frontend)
items.description: Concrete WonderlandAgent. Frontend implementation. Argues with Tweedledum via OpenAPI/contract speech acts.

items.title: Tweedledum agent (backend)
items.description: Concrete WonderlandAgent. Backend implementation. Counterpart to Tweedledee. Argues constantly; healthy by design.

items.title: Synthetic-consensus guard instrumentation
items.description: Per WONDERLAND_SPEC §7. Detect when an agent who would normally raise a concern softens or omits it under perceived deadline pressure. Constitutional-level guard plus bus-level audit (compare current dissent rate to historical baseline).

items.title: Per-character artifact handlers
items.description: Each character produces characteristic artifacts: tickets (Rabbit), ADRs (Cat), test scenarios (Hatter), reviews (Caterpillar), rulings (Queen), runbooks (Dormouse), implementations (Tweedles). Each handler validates shape and writes to .wonderland/.

items.title: Showcase 2: translation chat MVP
items.description: Headline showcase per WONDERLAND_SPEC §10. End-to-end translation-integrated chat app. Hatter finds a real bug. Cat redirects a Tweedle's overengineering. Recorded transcript with annotations.

items.title: Showcase 3: security recovery
items.description: Failure case showcase per §10. Queen catches security issue late, work is undone, Rabbit re-plans. Demonstrates real software entropy is handled, not papered over.

items.title: Showcase 4: multi-session persistence
items.description: Long-running thread across multiple sessions. Same agents, same memory, picking up where left off. Demonstrates persistence is doing real work — not theatrical.

items.title: Transcript annotation tooling
items.description: Render a thread of utterances with character voice, speech_act type, affect cues, dissent records inline. Used to publish showcases legibly. Markdown output.

items.title: Eval harness: generic baseline vs Wonderland
items.description: Per WONDERLAND_SPEC §11/§12. Same directive run through (a) generic role-prompted agents and (b) Wonderland. Score: bug-finding rate, architectural coherence, improvement curve over repeated runs. The compounding curve is the thesis evidence.

items.title: Token/cost telemetry and budgeting
items.description: Per WONDERLAND_SPEC §11 mitigation. Track tokens per agent per thread. Alert on runaway loops. Dashboard for per-directive cost so we can confirm engagement_policy is actually saving inference.

items.title: Cost analysis: Haiku-no-cache vs Sonnet-with-cache
items.description: Once the full agent workflow is running across showcases (P6), instrument and compare per-directive token costs for: (a) current default — Haiku 4.5 with cache_control markers that don't fire below ~4096 tokens; (b) Sonnet 4.6 which caches at ~2000 tokens and gives 0.10x reads. Anthropic pricing — Haiku ~$1/M input, Sonnet ~$3/M. Cached Sonnet wins per-call but uncached Haiku may win per-directive depending on cache-hit rate, which depends on average turns-per-thread. Decide based on real numbers, not intuition. See D-005 follow-up for the measured Haiku thresholds.

items.title: Cost-benefit analysis: Haiku 3.5 vs Haiku 4.5 for low-stakes calls
items.description:
Haiku 4.5 ($1.00/MTok in, $5.00/MTok out) is the default per the project's small-model thesis (project_haiku_thesis). Haiku 3.5 is $0.80/MTok in / $4.00/MTok out — 20% cheaper across the board. For high-frequency, structurally-bounded calls the older model may be sufficient. Candidates worth assessing per-call:

- **Engagement-gate decisions**: currently the §III rules are pure code (no LLM); but a future hybrid where a cheap model does an initial 'should I engage?' pass before the per-character protocol fires would offload most of the silence-choice cost to Haiku 3.5.
- **Compaction**: between-thread reflection per WONDERLAND_SPEC §8. Less time-pressured, mostly summarization of an existing transcript — quality bar is lower than per-turn deliberation.
- **Conflict-domain classification**: T19's domain-routing in the composition flow is a structured 'what domain is this?' classification, naturally fits a smaller model.
- **Procedural utterance generation**: the Dodo's nudge/acknowledgment templates are currently mechanical; if/when they go LLM-shaped, Haiku 3.5 is probably enough.

This is sibling work to roadmap item 460b5ea9 (Haiku-no-cache vs Sonnet-with-cache). Both fold into a per-call model-selection design where each agent's deliberate() can route to a different model based on the call's character. Run after P6's T34 telemetry lands so we have real per-call cost data to reason against.

Methodology: pick 2-3 candidate call sites (engagement-gate first, compaction second), run each with both 3.5 and 4.5, measure: (a) cost delta per call, (b) decision-quality delta (does 3.5 produce noticeably worse silence/non-silence calls? noticeably worse compaction summaries?). The thesis question parallel to the main one: identity-native + cheap-model is the same kind of bet as identity-native + small-model. Test it with data, not opinion.

items.title: Hard budget cap: refuse new agent turns once budget exceeded
items.description: Smoke test ran $0.59 against $0.30 budget — 2x overshoot. Budget cap is currently soft: many in-flight LLM calls return after the threshold trips, and the team continues working on the relayed directive until timeout. Hard cap requires gating WonderlandAgent.run() loops on Telemetry.total_cost > budget_dollars. Invasive change — touches every agent. Defer until after at least one showcase ships so we have more cost-overshoot data points.

items.title: Distinguish budget-exceeded brief from polite-deadlock brief in Dodo.escalate_deadlock
items.description: Smoke test surfaced this: when budget exceeded triggers _escalate_via_runner, the brief still says 'Thread has been STUCK (budget exceeded: $0.31 > $0.30)'. The parenthetical reason is right but the leading STUCK framing is wrong — there's no nudge ladder in this case, no polite deadlock pattern to surface. Two options: (a) add a budget_exceeded_brief() variant in Dodo, or (b) parameterize escalate_deadlock to dispatch on reason kind. Small fix, clear scope.

items.title: Tune framework primer to reduce procedural-caution chattiness
items.description: Smoke test data (cli-smoke run 20260505T152816, 90s, 10 agents): 47 of 54 visible utterances were question (27) or concern (20). Only 7 substantive artifacts produced; 1 nudge fired. Same 'before I X, I need Y from Z' pattern from analyses 006/007 in different clothes — agents are very procedurally cautious about acting. Three primer candidates likely amplifying: (a) §II lines 124-127 frames concern/question as conversation-starting moves with 'Choose deliberately' priming high-stakes preamble; (b) §VIII lines 307-308 has 'surface what only you can surface' getting vivid framing while silence guidance is three words; (c) §I cast table lists 'characteristic move' as present-active verb for each agent, priming demonstration of the move. Also worth investigating: §VII failure-modes summary may induce performative compensation. Test approach: A/B same directive with current primer vs. trimmed primer (sequence: trim §II commentary first as least invasive, measure question/concern ratio). Need to preserve T32's cache-padding effect — primer can shrink as long as combined prefix stays above 7000 tokens.

items.title: Per-agent allowed speech acts surfaced in primer
items.description: T36 surfaced 5 different agents (Caterpillar, Rabbit, Hatter, Tweedledee, Dormouse) trying to use Dodo-only speech acts (composition, nudge, acknowledgment) — each rejected at parse time, dropped to silence, ate substantive moves. Cause: framework primer §II lists ALL speech acts without per-agent restriction; LLM doesn't see each agent's per-Response Literal. Fix shape: parameterize FRAMEWORK_PRIMER with the agent's allowed substantive acts, OR add a per-agent allowed-acts callout in each agent's output protocol. Small, surgical. Eliminates ~6 dropped substantive moves per full-cast run.

items.title: Cat / Rabbit calibration: ship the artifact rather than re-clarifying
items.description: T36 surfaced load-bearing failure: Cat made 30 LLM calls / $0.94, shipped 0 ADRs (1 'proposal' speech act with prose, no artifact). Rabbit made 27 calls / $0.80, shipped 0 tickets. Both got stuck choosing concern/question instead of committing to their characteristic artifact. The Cat's §VIII (false certainty / refusing to commit / speaking to be present) showed up in real form. Possibly a new constitutional clause: 'after N turns of clarification on a topic in your domain, the next move is to commit even with confidence intervals.' Constitutions are text and can be tuned. Critical because without Cat ADRs and Rabbit tickets, the downstream Tweedles never reach the point where tool integration would matter.

items.title: Queen process-policing instead of substantive ruling
items.description: T36 surfaced: Queen shipped 3 rulings, all about team process ('architectural decision must precede X', 'decision-ownership must be visible'), zero security/compliance rulings on the actual surface (GDPR data retention, prompt injection, deletion-vs-chat-history conflict — all explicitly in the directive and Hatter's scenarios). Possibly a new §VIII clause: 'process-policing as substitute for substantive ruling when the substantive answer requires architectural context the Cat hasn't shipped.' Related to but distinct from the Cat-shipping issue — Queen had the information and chose process-meta over substance.

items.title: LLMClient backoff/retry on RateLimitError
items.description: T36 hit Anthropic 1M-tok/min org rate limit 40 times in 5 minutes (Queen 9, Dormouse 7, Caterpillar 7, Hatter 5, Cat 5, Rabbit 3, Tweedledum 3, Alice 1). Each hit dropped to silence — hard to disentangle 'agent chose silence' from 'agent rate-limited into silence' in the transcript. Add backoff + retry in LLMClient.complete on 429s. Useful regardless of multi-agent concurrency since any high-volume scenario will hit this.

items.title: Dodo decides kickoff meeting roster autonomously from directive content
items.description: Per the roster-architecture rollout (P6.T36 prep): initial implementation has the directive author specify the kickoff roster (option 1a), which is the simpler shape. The longer-term version (1b) is the Dodo reading the directive and deciding which agents to convene — e.g., 'this directive has GDPR + architectural questions → convene Alice + Cat + Queen for scoping, schedule Tweedles + Rabbit for after the ADR ships'. Adds one LLM call upfront but matches how a real PM/orchestrator works. Wait until 1a is in production and we have data on how often the directive author gets the roster wrong before building 1b.

items.title: Caterpillar maintains shared project memory (codex)
items.description: Per Kohl's framing during Block 2c: have Caterpillar maintain a markdown overview at .wonderland/codex.md (or similar) — a living 'what's actually built vs pending' document that all agents can consult. Solves three problems: (1) agents retreading worn ground (proposing things already built), (2) honesty about completion state (pending vs done), (3) shared situational awareness across meetings without each agent having to re-derive from episodic memory. Caterpillar is the natural maintainer because reviews surface the actual implementation surface, and he's already a 'read slowly' character. Design questions: (a) when does Caterpillar update — after each review? On a schedule? When a new file lands? (b) Schema — what sections (modules / contracts shipped / open ADRs / known gaps)? (c) How do other agents consume — auto-included in context like the framework primer? (d) Calibration to keep Caterpillar maintaining the codex from becoming PM. This wants tool integration for Caterpillar (which is now in flight) as a prerequisite — he needs read_file + write_file at minimum. Worth doing AFTER the full T36 enchilada test so the codex schema is informed by what an actual multi-meeting flow produces.

items.title: Revisit Cat STORY filter + Rabbit ADR framing bias
items.description:
Cat's STORY engagement is filter-deaf: cheshire_cat.py:119 selectively engages on STORY only when body matches {real-time, multi-tenant, offline, cross-language}. Stories about user roles (polyglot moderator, deaf user, GDPR trust) don't trip the filter, so Cat never synthesizes an ADR from the cumulative story picture — he waits for an architectural-keyword story or a concern/question with architectural smell.

Rabbit (white_rabbit.py:106) engages always on Alice stories, but his ticket vocabulary refracts through whatever ADR is in context. Same stories produce processor-boundary tickets when ADR present (v8) vs user-flow tickets when ADR absent (v9).

Stakes: T36 enchilada v9 showed this is load-bearing. When Cat doesn't ship an ADR in M1 (coin-flip behavior — v7/v9 silent, v8 shipped), the whole pipeline collapses: M3 Tweedles see no architectural anchor and return silence (2 calls, 0 contracts). M4/M5 starve. Cat's STORY filter determines whether the arc functions end-to-end.

Open questions: (1) broaden architectural_primitive_in_story vocabulary, or (2) add a separate selectively(STORY) rule that fires when N stories accumulate without an ADR, or (3) lift the synthesis responsibility into a different agent move. Whichever fix, the principle is: an ADR synthesizing across multiple user stories is a real architectural move and the framework currently can't make it.

items.title: Wire git identity (user.email, user.name) through wonderland config
items.description:
_ensure_git_repo() in src/wonderland/runner.py currently hardcodes `user.email=wonderland@local` and `user.name=Wonderland Runner` via `git config` (local scope) so the empty initial commit succeeds on systems without a global git config. These should flow through wonderland's config layer (the same JSON used for API keys, model overrides, etc.) so projects can attribute wonderland-generated commits to a specific identity (e.g., `Wonderland on behalf of <user>`).

Surfaced during analysis 016 followup when adding the git_status/git_diff tool surface for Caterpillar reviews.

items.title: Revisit ignoring .wonderland/ in generated repos
items.description:
_ensure_git_repo() in src/wonderland/runner.py writes a default .gitignore that excludes .wonderland/ from version control. Reasoning: registry writes (memory sqlite, telemetry, stories/adr/contract markdown) would otherwise pollute git_status / git_diff and bury the actual code changes the Caterpillar reviews.

But: a side-benefit of being mostly markdown-document-based is that artifacts CAN be version-controlled — stories, ADRs, contract notes, rulings, reviews are all .md files. Versioning those alongside code would give the team a real audit trail (git blame on the ADR; git log on the contract). Episodic memory sqlite would still need to be ignored (binary, frequently-changed), and telemetry json is per-run noise. So the right rule is probably: ignore .wonderland/{memory,telemetry}/ but track .wonderland/{stories,architecture,tickets,contract-notes,rulings,implementations,reviews}/.

Side question: does Caterpillar reading prior ADRs/contracts via git history change his review behavior? Probably yes.

items.title: Dodo as dynamic meeting orchestrator (big rework)
items.description:
Substrate redesign making Dodo the dynamic orchestrator of meeting chains, not just the convener-of-already-set-up meetings.

Scope:
- Dynamic meeting chains: Dodo decides what meeting comes next based on what the prior meeting shipped (M1 produced stories+ADR → M2 needs Rabbit + the ADR/stories as seeds, with a decomposition directive). Today this is hard-coded in the test scripts.
- Per-agent deliberation tracking: Dodo subscribes to a 'deliberation_started' / 'deliberation_finished' signal and holds the meeting open while expected responses are pending. Replaces the fixed-quantum quiescence threshold.
- Late-deliberation handling: when a slow deliberation completes after its trigger's thread closed, route the utterance to the currently-active thread or a 'lost-utterance' bucket rather than silently publishing into a closed thread.
- Escalation interleaving: Dodo can pause a meeting to escalate to a human and resume cleanly when the human responds (relevant for T37 security recovery).

Origin: T36 enchilada v17 had Tweedle tools-loop deliberations take >30s; M3 quiesced before responses landed; contract_notes published into a closed thread and were lost from capture. Workaround: bumped quiescence_seconds from 30 to 60 in the script (helps but doesn't solve — some deliberations take >60s too).

Stop-gap done as separate small slice: late-deliberation detection + warning + lost-utterance registry, so silent-data-loss can't happen mid-diagnosis. Stop-gap is a Runner-side substrate fix, not Dodo work; the big Dodo rework supersedes it eventually.

Don't start the big rework until T37 reveals what its meeting shape actually needs from dynamic orchestration — the security-recovery showcase will surface requirements (escalation interleaving, conflict ladder, non-linear meeting chains) that should inform the design.

items.title: Scaffolding-as-feature: project-skeleton templates
items.description:
Real engineers don't argue about which test framework to use on day 1 — they `cookiecutter`, they `create-react-app`, they `django-admin startproject`. The Wonderland team should make the choices that *matter* (architecture, contracts, behavior, what to ship) and inherit the choices that don't (project structure, build config, test runner, basic HTTP framework, DB connection scaffolding). Generating boilerplate via LLM calls is expensive AND wasteful AND introduces variability where there shouldn't be any.

Originated from T37 v3 → T38 planning: T37 surfaced that pre-seeding a real codebase dramatically improves output quality (analysis 019). T38 needs a fullstack skeleton so Session 1 builds features ON TOP of a known foundation; Session 2/3 can then meaningfully reference what got built in Session 1 because the foundation shape is stable across runs.

Minimum-viable shape:
  src/wonderland/templates/
    fullstack-fastapi-react/    # backend + frontend (T38)
    python-fastapi-sqlite/      # backend-only
    react-vite-typescript/      # frontend-only
    python-cli/                 # click + pytest

Surface:
  - `wonderland scaffold <project_root> --template <name>` CLI
  - `wonderland.scaffold.lay_down_template(...)` programmatic
  - Optional `template=` kwarg on `Runner.make_full_cast`

The T37 seed pattern (analyses/data/019-security-recovery-seed/, the showcase script's _commit_seed_baseline helper) is the prototype. Promotion to first-class is mostly: factor out the copy + git-init logic, add a few canonical templates, wire the CLI/Runner.

Start with the fullstack template (T38 needs it). Other templates can land as showcases need them; no need to speculate.

items.title: Local-model router for substrate calls (Ollama)
items.description:
Route rote, non-identity-bearing LLM calls to a local Ollama instance to keep development costs down. Anthropic stays the default for any call that produces an Utterance (identity-bearing); local handles substrate.

Candidate call sites (in rough leverage order):
1. Inter-thread compaction (Cat's reflection on closed threads → memory entries). High volume, fixed schema, no Utterance produced.
2. Tool-result digestion (read_file / git_diff / list_files outputs pre-summarized before they ride into the next agent call). Cuts input tokens dramatically.
3. Synthetic-consensus guard observations (judge-style call against the §11 anti-pattern).
4. Test-scenario expansion (Hatter's per-scenario fleshing once skeletons exist).

NOT candidates: any agent's main response (constitutions encode behavior the local model wasn't trained on — routing them defeats the thesis), engagement decisions (constitutional), and ANY call inside P7 eval runs.

Implementation shape:
- New ModelRouter with strategies keyed by call-site enum (COMPACTION, TOOL_DIGEST, JUDGE, AGENT_RESPONSE, etc.).
- Feature-flagged via env var (WONDERLAND_LOCAL_ROUTER=1 or per-site flags); default off.
- Local model config slot in ~/.config/wonderland/config.json alongside the Anthropic block (base_url, model name, timeout).
- Hard requirement: P7 eval harness MUST refuse to start if local router is on, to keep the comparison clean.

Hardware target: Kohl's 4070Ti Super (16GB VRAM) — fits Qwen2.5-Coder 14B Q4, Llama 3.1 8B Q8, or Mistral Small 22B Q4.

Risks: model parity (Ollama models follow instructions differently than Haiku — substrate calls may need provider-specific prompts), hallucination on substrate calls poisoning the bus, more debugging surface. Mitigation: opt-in per call site, validate outputs against the same pydantic schemas Anthropic responses use, fall back to Anthropic on validation failure.

items.title: Split max_tool_iterations: read tools don't increment counter
items.description:
Currently `max_tool_iterations` (in `agent._complete_with_tools`) is a flat cap on ALL tool calls — read_file, list_files, git_status, git_diff, write_file all count equally. This conflates two different kinds of risk:

- Write tools (write_file): real side effects. Capping iterations is genuinely protective against runaway writes.
- Read tools (read_file, list_files, git_status, git_diff): pure lookups. The risk is cost, not correctness, and `budget_dollars` is already the right backstop for that.

The pathology: a continuation Tweedle on a 30-file codebase (e.g. Session 2 of T38) burns 12 read iterations on exploration before designing — leaving only 8 write iterations for shipping. Greenfield Tweedles don't pay this tax because they have nothing to read; they go straight to writing. The cap penalizes the more disciplined behavior (read existing code first) over the less disciplined one (just start writing).

Cleanest fix: exclude pure-read tools from the iteration counter entirely. Counter becomes 'operations with side effects.' Budget cap handles read-runaway via $.

Implementation:
- Define READ_ONLY_TOOLS = {'read_file', 'list_files', 'git_status', 'git_diff'} in agent.py
- In `_complete_with_tools`, only increment iteration counter when the tool name is NOT in READ_ONLY_TOOLS
- Keep max_tool_iterations default at 20 (consequential moves only); reads bounded by budget cap

Why no second cap: avoids another knob to tune (we already have iter cap + budget + per-meeting cap + quiescence timeout); semantically cleaner.

Validation: re-run T38 Session 2 after this change; expect Tweedles to read existing files freely AND ship code, where pre-fix they hit iter exhaustion mid-exploration in analysis 020. Will be visible as a comparison point in analysis 022 territory.

Defer until after analyses 021 ships — don't change substrate mid-test.

items.title: Consolidate contract-negotiation + implementation into one meeting
items.description:
Merge M3 (contract-negotiation) and M4 (implementation) in the canonical T36/T38-shaped sequence into a single 'design-and-ship' meeting. The Tweedles already do this work as one continuous flow — the M3/M4 split is an a priori boundary the system keeps voting against.

Evidence (from analysis 020 and the analysis 021 territory T38 Session 1 re-run):
- M3 produces state=proposed contracts, then Tweedles immediately start implementation in turn 2 (write_file via tools)
- M3 quiesces and closes mid-tool-loop; the resulting implementation utterance is suppressed as late-publish
- Backend code lands on disk (write_file is a side-effect that completes regardless), but the implementation utterance is lost
- M4 then opens with no fresh signal because Tweedles already 'moved past' M3 — M4 ships zero implementation utterances and closes empty

What separation was supposed to give us:
- Frozen-seam checkpoint: 'contracts agreed, now implement' — never actually reached in practice; per-meeting budget caps fire first
- No-tools vs tools-on tool surface — never enforced (Tweedles have write_file in both meetings)
- Cross-meeting composition test point — already covered by ADR (M1) → tickets (M2) handoff

What consolidation gives us:
- No meeting-boundary leak (the bug class disappears)
- Matches actual engineering work (design-the-seam-while-shipping is one thought)
- Tweedledee's restraint becomes visible (waits for backend Tweedle in same meeting instead of waiting across closed meetings)
- Simpler budget math (one ~$1.80 cap instead of two awkwardly-handed-off caps)

What's preserved:
- contract_note artifacts with proposed/agreed states (state transition lives at artifact level, not meeting level)
- Future sessions still read agreed contracts from registry
- Caterpillar's M5 review surface unchanged (reviews diff against HEAD; doesn't care which meeting produced it)

Implementation: script change, not framework change. Edit the canonical T36/T38 templates to use a single 'design-and-ship' meeting between decomposition and review. Quiescence/budget tuned for the longer meeting (need turn-based quiescence — separate roadmap item — for this to be safe). Framework still supports separated M3/M4 if some other use case wants it.

Validation target: T38 re-run produces frontend AND backend code, contracts at state=agreed in the registry, no late-publish suppressions, M5 review on the full diff.

items.title: Turn-based quiescence detection (replace wall-clock)
items.description:
Replace wall-clock quiescence detection with turn-based per-agent state tracking. Agents are turn-based entities; using elapsed-since-last-event to decide 'the team is done' is a category error that we've been band-aiding with ever-growing timeouts (30s → 60s → would need 120s for tool turns → 180s for chained tool loops → still race-prone).

The Runner already knows all the state internally — it's literally awaiting the agents' coroutines. It just doesn't expose this state to the thread monitor, which falls back to wall-clock because that's all it can see.

Per-agent state machine the thread monitor should track:
- IDLE — received an utterance, engagement rule said no, no pending work
- ENGAGED_PENDING — engagement rule fired, awaiting first LLM call
- IN_TOOL_LOOP — _complete_with_tools is currently iterating
- AWAITING_RESPONSE — LLM call in flight, no tools yet
- COMPLETING — LLM responded, finalizing artifact synthesis + publish

Thread quiescence = |agents not in IDLE| == 0 AND a tiny settling window (~2-5s wall-clock, just to catch the race where an agent's engagement decision is mid-flight). 

Wall-clock survives in two narrower, semantically-distinct roles:
1. Settling window (2-5s after last state transition)
2. Stuck-detection TIMEOUT (not quiescence). 'Team finished' vs 'team hung' are different terminations and should be distinct events on the bus.

Implementation:
- New AgentState enum + per-agent state map on Runner (or a dedicated AgentMonitor)
- Hooks at: utterance-received → engagement-decided → llm-call-start → tool-loop-enter → tool-loop-exit → publish-complete
- ThreadMonitor subscribes to AgentMonitor state-change events instead of polling for new bus events
- New event kinds: 'agent_engaged', 'agent_idle', 'agent_in_tool_loop'
- The existing 'quiescent' state transition becomes derived: emit when all agents IDLE for >settling-window
- New 'stuck' state transition: emit when any agent has been in non-IDLE for >stuck-timeout (default 5min)

Composes with the M3+M4 consolidation: combined meeting + turn-based quiescence = meeting stays open exactly as long as anyone is doing work, closes the moment the team is genuinely done. No more late-publish suppressions, no more mid-turn closures.

Touches: src/wonderland/runner.py (thread monitor, the convene/events loop), src/wonderland/agent.py (state-change hooks at tool-loop entry/exit), and the script-side render_event for the new event kinds.

Validation: T38 re-run after this lands should show zero late-publish suppressions and zero meetings closing while a Tweedle is mid-tool-loop.

items.title: Daedalus-as-agent: Claude Code as Wonderland implementation backend
items.description:
Bridge Wonderland and Daedalus into one development platform. Allow Wonderland's Runner to delegate certain agent turns (initially the Tweedles for implementation work) to a local Claude Code session instead of the Anthropic API.

Motivation:
- User holds a Claude Max subscription (unlimited usage within rate limits) — implementation work via API burns tokens that are 'free' via Max
- Daedalus already has filesystem + git tooling, makes implementation work natural
- Positions Wonderland as the design committee and Daedalus as the IC: different cognitive modes for different work types
- Tweedles are the natural handoff point — they're the implementation pair, and Daedalus is already a builder/craftsman

Open design questions (to resolve when this work is picked up):
- Identity tension: Tweedles have constitutions with characteristic asymmetry (Tweedledum eager-implementer / Tweedledee restraint-first). Does Daedalus play the character authentically, or is the Tweedle costume just an interface for shipping code?
- This explicitly violates the haiku_thesis (small model + strong constitution) for the agent role being played — only acceptable as a development-time accelerator, not as the production architecture
- IPC channel: how does the Runner signal a turn to Claude Code? File-based handoff? Local socket? MCP? CLI subprocess?
- Which agents are eligible: just Tweedles (implementation) or also Caterpillar (review)? Probably not Alice/Cat/Queen — their value is character-driven judgment, less suited to Daedalus's role
- Composition with the Ollama router (0aab0178): both are 'route some calls elsewhere' — share infrastructure?

This is the long-term cohesion vision, not urgent. File for when Wonderland is more stable and the cost-of-API-development becomes the binding constraint.

items.title: Parse-error retry: one LLM re-prompt before treating as silence
items.description:
When deliberate() raises a *ResponseParseError (Queen/Tweedles/Cat/etc. all have their own variant), the speak loop currently catches it and treats the turn as silence — see the 'treating as silence' stderr message. The turn is lost: the LLM produced a substantive response, our parser couldn't read it, the agent stays silent, the bus moves on without their input.

Recurring failure mode across analyses 020, 021, 022. Cost in 022's M1: ~120s of dead wall-clock time on a single Queen parse error (this softens with turn-based quiescence in commit 305d3b2 but the lost turn itself remains).

Proposed fix: one retry on parse error before falling back to silence. The retry prompt feeds the original prompt PLUS the malformed response PLUS a one-line directive ('your previous response was malformed JSON; respond again with valid JSON matching the schema'). If the retry also fails, fall back to silence (current behavior). Costs at most one additional LLM call per parse error; recovers the turn the substantial majority of the time.

Implementation surface:
- Each agent's deliberate() has its own parse step that raises a ResponseParseError. Either:
  (a) Add retry logic in each agent's deliberate (per-character), OR
  (b) Add a shared retry helper in agent.py that wraps a parse-and-retry pattern, OR
  (c) Add the retry at the speak() loop level — catch ResponseParseError, re-call deliberate with a hint
  Option (b) feels cleanest: a _complete_with_retry helper alongside _complete_with_tools.

- Cap retries at 1 by default. More than that risks runaway cost on a genuinely malformed prompt.

- Track retry count in telemetry so we can measure how often retries succeed vs fail.

- Consider whether the brace-balanced JSON fallback in parsing.py already handles some cases — there may be overlap. Ensure the retry only fires when the fallback also failed.

Composition with existing fixes:
- Turn-based quiescence (305d3b2) reduces the *cost* of parse errors (no 60s wall-clock tax) but doesn't recover the lost turn. This item recovers the turn.
- Consolidation (script-level, no commit) reduces the surface area where lost turns matter (fewer meeting boundaries). Doesn't address parse errors directly.

This is the third leg of closing the 'Tweedles don't ship' bug class — quiescence + parse retry + consolidation together should make the runs reliable.

items.title: Turn-based quiescence: race between agent IDLE and pending trigger
items.description:
Residual issue from the turn-based quiescence rework (305d3b2). When an agent has multiple triggers queued, there's a race window between processing turn N and picking up trigger N+1:

  1. Agent finishes deliberating turn N, publishes utterance, enters speak()'s finally block
  2. Agent's _set_state(IDLE) fires
  3. Monitor sees all members IDLE, fires QUIESCENT
  4. Dodo emits acknowledgment, thread transitions to COMPLETE
  5. Agent's speak() loops back to gather_triggers, picks up queued trigger N+1
  6. Agent enters AWAITING_RESPONSE, deliberates, tries to publish — late-publish suppression fires

Observed in analysis 023's runs: 2-3 events per run, typically Tweedles responding to each other's contract proposals after M3 closed. The lost utterances are usually 'extras' (ancillary commentary) rather than load-bearing artifacts.

Fix candidates:
- (a) speak()'s finally only sets IDLE when self.pending.empty(). Avoids the race in the common case (multiple triggers queued mid-turn).
- (b) listen()'s should_engage path sets state AWAITING_RESPONSE when it puts on pending — declares engagement before speak() picks up.
- (c) Both. Defense in depth.

Recommendation: start with (a) — minimal change, addresses the common case. If late-publish events persist, add (b).

Cost of leaving unfixed: a few utterances per run get lost. Per the working-tree-as-implementation-artifact framing, code shipping is what matters, not utterance preservation. Polish item, not load-bearing.
